+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in New Orleans hits me like a wet wool blanket pulled straight from a dryer. It smells like stale chicory, river mud, and piss. The trucker who gave me a ride from Meridian had shoved me out at a red light somewhere near Canal Street with a muttered, *“End of the line, kid,”* before I could even grab my jacket off the floorboards. So now I’m standing on a cracked sidewalk, watching his rusted taillights bleed into the morning haze, shivering in eighty-degree heat. The left strap of my canvas backpack slips off my shoulder. I yank it back up. It immediately slides down again. The nylon webbing is frayed to hell, the plastic buckle snapped three months ago when I kicked it down the basement stairs back in Pigeon Forge. Pigeon Forge. God, even thinking the name makes my throat close up. Forty-eight hours ago, I was still sitting across the kitchen table from Mom, watching her face curdle. *“Concerning behavioural patterns,”* Mr. Harrison, the smug prick of a guidance counselor, had called it. He thought my acting out was about Dad leaving, or pot, or bad grades. He didn’t know shit. None of them did. Until I told them. *I’m trans,* I’d said, voice shaking like an autumn leaf in an exhaust fan. *I can’t do this girl routine anymore. I’m done.* Mom didn’t scream. That was the worst part. She just sighed, this heavy, disgusted sound, like I was a glass of spilled milk she didn’t want to wipe up, and said, *“I can’t deal with another one of your stunts, Taylor. You’re sick. We’ll call Harrison back on Monday.”* There was no Monday. Monday was thirty minutes to stuff three t-shirts, a binder, fifty-four dollars, and an apple into a broken bag, climbing out the bathroom window before the sun came up. Now I’m here. And I have exactly twenty-two dollars left. The strap slips again. I hitch it violently, glaring at a trio of tourists sipping neon-colored slushes out of plastic bongs. Nobody looks back. In Tennessee, I took up too much space just by breathing. Here, I’m invisible. It should feel like freedom, but it tastes like panic. My pulse is a hammer against my ribs. By midday, the humidity has turned my t-shirt into a second skin. My feet burn inside my beat-up Converse. I drift toward a patch of green surrounded by black iron spikes—Jackson Square, a sign says. The park is full of fortune tellers, brass players, and pigeons fat as bowling balls. I drop onto a low stone bench near an overgrown magnolia tree, pulling my knees to my chest. *What the fuck did you do, Taylor?* my brain screams. *You have no place to sleep. You don’t know anyone. What if they call the cops? What if Mom doesn’t even care enough to report you missing?* “You’re gonna get your shit boosted if you keep staring into space like that.” I jump, my head whipping around. Leaning against the brick pillar behind me is a kid who looks maybe seventeen, rail-thin, drowning in an oversized denim vest pinned with rusted bottle caps. Short, choppy black hair, dark circles bruised beneath sharp hazel eyes, and a strip of athletic tape wrapped tight around their right knuckles. “I’m not staring,” I snap, voice cracking slightly. Defensive, stupid, pure instinct. The kid snorts, pushing off the pillar and sauntering over. They drop onto the opposite end of the bench with the fluid grace of an alley cat. “Right. You’re just meditating on the beauty of concrete. Look at you. Fresh off the interstate. You reek of diesel and panic.” “I don’t reek of anything.” I hitch the backpack strap up my shoulder again. It slides right back down to my elbow. The kid watches the strap, amused. “That bag’s fighting you harder than a parish deputy. I’m Remy.” “Taylor.” “Taylor,” Remy repeats, tasting it. “No last name. Smart. Means you’re either dodging parents or parole.” “Parents,” I mutter, staring at my shoes. “Always the parents.” Remy digs into their vest pocket, pulls out a half-crushed pack of generic smokes, and sticks one between their lips without lighting it. Their hands are shaking just a fraction. I notice a faint, fresh scab slicing across their jawline. “Tennessee?” My head snaps up. “How did you—” “The twang, genius. You stretch your vowels like saltwater taffy.” Remy glances over my head, eyes scanning the square. Not casually, either. It’s a rhythmic, paranoid sweep—cop cars, park rangers, guys in dark glasses. “You got people here?” “No.” “Money?” “Some,” I lie. Remy laughs, a dry, raspy sound. “Right. You’re loaded. That’s why you’re sitting on a damp bench looking like a kicked puppy.” They lean in a little, lowering their voice. The amusement fades, replaced by something brittle and razor-sharp. “Listen to me, Taylor. New Orleans eats runaways for breakfast and spits out empty wallets and coroner reports. You wander Frenchmen Street after dark looking like a lost deer, somebody’s gonna offer you a warm bed, and by morning you’ll wish you were dead. You get me?” A chill cuts through the swampy heat. My stomach roils. “Why do you care?” Remy looks away, staring up into the twisted branches of the magnolia. Their jaw tightens, muscle ticking over that nasty scab. “Maybe I don’t. Maybe I just hate seeing tourists waste good bench space.” They pause, chewing on the unlit filter. “Or maybe three days ago I was the idiot sitting where you’re sitting, thinking I was out of the woods.” “What happened three days ago?” I ask, leaned forward despite myself. Remy’s eyes snap back to mine, dark and guarded. “Let’s just say there’s an angry foster dad in Baton Rouge with a fractured nose and my name on a missing persons file. And if he finds me before I make enough cash to catch a bus to Texas, I’m not going back to a group home. I’m going to a juvenile facility.” I swallow hard. Back home, my drama felt earth-shattering. My mom’s cold disgust, the silent rooms, the dread of existing in the wrong skin. But sitting next to Remy, the world suddenly feels massive, vicious, and completely indifferent to a sixteen-year-old’s heartbreak. “I came out,” I blurt out, not even knowing why. “To my family. They looked at me like I was a freak.” Remy doesn’t laugh. They take the cigarette out of their mouth and look at me—really look at me—taking in my oversized hoodie, my cropped hair, the desperate tension coiled in my spine. “You ain’t a freak,” Remy says, voice entirely devoid of sarcasm for the first time. “You’re just early. Takes people a long time to catch up. Most of ‘em never do.” The sun is dipping low now, casting long, bruised-purple shadows across the square. The brass band down the alley kicks into a loud, syncopated jazz standard, trumpets blaring into the dusk. Streetlamps hum to life, flickering against the falling dark. I’m terrified. Truly, deeply terrified. My ribs ache from my binder, my stomach is completely empty, and I don’t know where I’m going to close my eyes tonight. The strap of my backpack slips off my shoulder again. This time, Remy reaches over, grabs the loose nylon tail, and ties it into a tight, ugly square knot against the upper loop. “There,” Remy says, standing up and stretching their bruised hands toward the neon glow of the street. “Won’t slip now. Come on, Tennessee. I know a place behind an abandoned bakery that has an awning and dry cardboard. You buy me a po’boy with that ‘fortune’ you got, and I’ll make sure nobody shanks you before sunrise.” I look at the dark shadows lengthening between the trees, then look at Remy. I don’t know if I can trust them. I don’t know if I’ll survive this week. I reach back, test the knot. It holds. “Deal,” I say, and I follow them into the neon night.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen runaway's first day in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a mix of vulnerability, defensiveness, and raw fear that feels genuine for a 16-year-old in crisis. The characterization is particularly effective. Taylor's internal monologue reveals layers of emotion - the fresh wound of family rejection, practical terror about survival, and the complex mix of invisibility and exposure that comes with being a runaway. The character of Remy is well-crafted as a street-smart foil who provides both danger and potential salvation, with their own mysterious backstory that adds intrigue without feeling forced. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, avoiding both overly polished speech and cartoonish slang. Remy's voice is distinct from Taylor's - more hardened and cynical but not without empathy. The conversation flows organically and reveals character through subtext. The sensory details of New Orleans are vivid without becoming overwrought - the "wet wool blanket" humidity, the specific smells, the visual details of Jackson Square. The setting feels authentic and contributes to the atmosphere of disorientation and danger. The pacing is well-controlled, moving from Taylor's immediate disorientation through the encounter with Remy to a tentative alliance. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - not falsely optimistic but offering a glimmer of hope and connection that feels earned given the characters' shared circumstances. The prose style effectively uses short, punchy sentences during moments of high emotion or action, contrasting with longer, more reflective passages during introspection. The mixed tense approach works well, creating immediacy while allowing for reflection. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphors feel slightly strained, and the backstory exposition, while necessary, sometimes interrupts the narrative flow. However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise strong piece. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
It is a well-documented law of the post-collapse landscape that if a man sets out to find a three-quarter-inch rubber washer, the universe will inevitably provide him with six tons of twisted rebar, an agitated badger, and dysentery. Midas knew this. He had the knees of a man who knew this, both of which made the sound of a dry branch snapping whenever he stood up. "The drip," Midas said, squinting through the cracked windscreen of their home—a 1998 Volvo estate deeply embedded in an overgrown rhododendron bush—"is psychological warfare. It goes *plink*. Then it waits until you think it’s not going to *plink*, and then it *plinks*." On the passenger dashboard, Chewy stared ahead with the unblinking, glassy serenity of a creature whose manufacturer had long since dissolved into atomic dust. Chewy was, nominally, a koala. In practice, he was six inches of matted acrylic pelt stretched over a brass clockwork chassis, missing his left ear and possessing a small internal speaker that crackled like frying bacon. A small whir of gears groaned behind Chewy’s polyester ribs. "*Four out of five dentists recommend it,*" Chewy said in a tinny, cheerful baritone, "*for a brighter, whiter tomorrow.*" "Quite," said Midas. "So we go to the Megamart. We search the Plumbing and Sanitary aisle. We secure one rubber washer. We avoid the Skag-Benders, we do not look at the feral geese, and we return before noon. A surgical strike." Chewy’s head clicked thirty degrees to the left. A glass eye fell out, bounced off the gearstick, and vanished into the footwell. Midas sighed, retrieved an old bit of chewed twine, and tied the eye back into its socket. "A tactical masterpiece. Let’s move." *** The ruins of the Megamart sat in the valley like the carcass of a beached, corrugated-iron whale. The world had ended some seventy years prior—nobody was entirely certain why, though general consensus blamed an update to terms and conditions that went horribly wrong—and nature had spent the intervening decades attempting to turn consumer electronics into potting soil. "Step lightly," Midas murmured, picking his way through the shattered remains of Seasonal Gardening. "The floor is mostly ceiling here." Chewy, wedged firmly into the breast pocket of Midas’s canvas coat, emitted a faint hum. "*Reduces unsightly bloating,*” he confided to the empty air. The Plumbing aisle was located just past Homewares, which was currently occupied by a family of screech-owls who held very conservative views on trespassing. Midas skirted them with the agonizing caution of a man walking over dry cornflakes in church. He reached the promised land: Bin 42, Fasteners and Gaskets. Suspended over the bin was a skeletal display rack, groaning under the weight of three rusted water heaters that had fallen from the mezzanine in the Great Collapse of ’41 and were currently held aloft by nothing more than oxidized pride and a single strip of perished strapping. Directly beneath it lay a small, black rubber ring. The Grail. "You see?" Midas whispered, his hand trembling as he reached forward. "Civilization is simply a matter of applied—" A rusted spring snapped with the acoustics of a sniper rifle. Chewy’s internal mechanism buzzed violently. "*Batteries not included!*" he shrieked at ninety decibels. "*Warning: Choking hazard!*" The screech-owls took this personally. What followed was not so much an escape as an aggressive recalculation of physics. The water heaters came down with a subterranean roar that pulverized Bin 42 into a fine red powder. The collapse brought down an overhead ventilation duct, which in turn disturbed a hive of mud-wasps that had been peacefully living inside a display model bread-maker since the late autumn. Midas, running entirely on panic and brittle bone, sprinted toward the exit. He tripped over a vintage mop bucket, did a frantic, three-legged dance that would have won accolades in a more avant-garde era of theatre, and plunged headlong through the drywall into an adjacent, unexplored territory: *The Great Beyond*. It was the outdoor sporting goods section. More specifically, it was the fishing tackle department. "Ow," Midas observed, rolling over. "*Side effects may include nausea, dizziness, and sudden death,*" Chewy remarked from his pocket, his small speaker vibrating against Midas’s ribs. "Shut up, Chewy." "Is that someone in the hooks?" a voice called out from the dark. It was a wet, phlegmy voice. It belonged to the sort of man who wore three hats simultaneously and considered roadkill an under-leveraged breakfast option. Midas froze. He was tangled in forty yards of high-tensile nylon monofilament and had three barbed spinners embedded in the calf of his trousers. From the shadows emerged two Skag-Benders, wielding sharpened curtain rods and grinning with the desperate enthusiasm of people who hadn't had a hobby in three generations. "Fresh leather," the larger one grunted, eying Midas’s boots. Midas looked down at his breast pocket. Chewy was clicking furiously. "My companion is a demon," Midas said, his voice cracking only twice. "A god of the Before. He eats souls. And… and plaque." The Skag-Benders paused, squinting at the lumpy, one-eyed stuffed animal. Chewy gave a sudden, convulsive shudder. A gear slipped. A capacitor sparked. "*Wazzup!*" Chewy roared, with the full, unholy acoustic force of an ancient optical-disc soundbite. "*Snap into a Slim Jim! Just DO IT!*" A spark shot out of Chewy's nose, directly into a puddle of lawnmower fuel that had sat undisturbed since the turn of the century. *** They returned to the Volvo at dusk. Midas was missing his left boot, having abandoned it to the monofilament and the fire. He was covered in soot, had an owl feather stuck firmly to the bridge of his nose via congealed tree sap, and was limping in a way that suggested his pelvis was now held together mostly by polite disagreement. He slumped into the driver's seat and leaned his head against the steering wheel. Beside him, Chewy was placed back onto the dashboard. The koala’s fur was now predominantly charred black, his single glass eye was dangling against his cheek like a monocle, and his clockwork inside sounded like a pocket watch dropped into a blender. *Plink.* Midas did not move. *Plink.* Slowly, carefully, Midas opened his clenched fist. Sitting in his soot-stained palm was a washer. It was half-melted, distinctly oval-shaped, and roughly three times the diameter of the kitchen pipe. *Plink.* Chewy let out a final, dying rasp of static. A puff of grey smoke leaked from his mouth. "*Because...*" the bear whispered, fading into the eternal twilight of dead electronics, "*...you're worth it.*" Midas closed his eyes. "Tomorrow," he said to the ceiling, "we look for tape."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and philosophical undertones wrapped in absurdist situations. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting while maintaining the light, satirical tone that characterizes Pratchett's work. The story structure adheres well to the prompt requirements: it opens with the characters planning their mission, follows them through escalating complications, and returns them home worse for wear. The mission's inevitable failure feels organic and well-orchestrated through a cascade of mishaps that build naturally from one disaster to the next. Midas emerges as a believable protagonist - world-weary, pragmatic, yet persistently hopeful despite repeated setbacks. His interactions with Chewy create genuine character moments, and his resigned acceptance of failure feels earned. Chewy, despite being an animatronic toy, becomes surprisingly endearing through his random advertising snippets that occasionally align with dramatic moments. The prose demonstrates considerable skill in balancing humor with genuine pathos. Lines like "Civilization is simply a matter of applied—" followed by immediate catastrophe exemplify the author's timing. The descriptive passages are vivid without becoming overwrought, particularly the Megamart's decay and the action sequences. The dialogue, while limited, serves its purpose effectively. Chewy's random commercial phrases provide consistent humor while occasionally achieving unexpected poignancy, especially his final "Because... you're worth it." Midas's sparse dialogue reveals character efficiently. The story maintains internal consistency and logical progression despite its absurdist elements. The world-building feels authentic to both the post-apocalyptic genre and Pratchett's sensibilities. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither artificially upbeat nor gratuitously dark, but realistically resigned with a hint of persistent human determination. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the Pratchett pastiche becomes slightly obvious, and a few descriptive passages that edge toward purple prose. The pacing occasionally rushes through potentially rich moments, particularly during the Skag-Bender encounter which could have been developed further. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the door didn’t just ring; it shrieked as the heavy oak was slammed shut against the Welsh drizzle. Outside, across the rain-slicked cobbles of the square, two figures with telephoto lenses skidded on the wet slate, cursing into the grey mist. Inside, Julian Fox collapsed back against the shut door, chest heaving beneath his drenched cashmere overcoat. He pulled off his dark glasses with a theatrical flourish, ran a hand through artfully ruined dark curls, and offered the empty shop a breathless, cinematic smirk. “Narrow thing,” he murmured. From behind the counter, half-buried behind a stack of local historical gazetteers, a dry voice replied, “Mind the umbrella stand. It’s Victorian, and it bites.” Julian blinked, adjusting his eyes to the amber gloom of the shop. She sat on a high stool, wearing an oversized cable-knit sweater the colour of moss and a pencil tucked behind an ear. She didn’t look up from her ledger. She didn't drop her pen. She didn't even gasp. Julian’s smile tightened by a fraction of a millimetre. A tiny, familiar tremor of panic—the cold little voice that whispered *they’re not looking at you*—grazed his ribs. He deployed the Fox Smile: the one that had carried him through three West End revivals and two blockbuster franchises. Slow, slightly lopsided, wickedly warm. “Terribly sorry about the intrusion,” he said, stepping forward. He let the resonant, velvet baritone do the heavy lifting. “A pack of hounds out there. Mind if I take sanctuary among the paperbacks for twenty minutes? I’m Julian, by the way.” The woman finally looked up. Her eyes were a sharp, hazel grey, completely unreadable. Inwardly, Gwenna’s heart did an absurd, terrifying leap into her throat. *Julian Fox.* It was ridiculous. He looked absurdly, offensively good in the dim Welsh rainlight—the jawline carved by someone who clearly took themselves very seriously, the scent of expensive bergamot and wet wool cutting right through the dust. Her pulse hammered in her wrists, but five generations of stubborn mountain stock refused to let her show it. She laid her pen down with deliberate slowness. “Twenty minutes is fine, Julian By-The-Way. Browsing fee is five pounds, or you actually buy a book.” Julian paused mid-stride. He gave an airy laugh, testing the waters. “A cover charge? For me?” “For anyone whose boots are currently tracking slate-mud onto my runner,” she said mildly. Julian glanced down. He was indeed leaving damp footprints. A hot prickle rushed up the back of his neck. *She doesn’t know who I am,* he thought, horrified. *Or worse, she does, and she finds me boring.* “Right,” he said, drawing nearer to the counter, leaning an elbow on the scarred mahogany. He tilted his head, holding her gaze with practiced, devastating intensity. “Let’s start over. I’m seeking refuge. You’re the enigmatic guardian of… ancient wisdom. Tell me, do you treat all your paying customers like errant schoolboys, or did I do something specifically to earn the honour?” Gwenna felt the heat rising in her collarbones. His eyes were entirely too bright, his presence crowding the small space between the counter and the poetry section. It made her want to smooth her hair; instead, she crossed her arms tightly over her chest. “I find the schoolboy approach keeps egos from bruising the woodwork,” she said. “Particularly the imported ones.” Julian’s charming smirk flickered. He straightened up, his velvet façade fraying just enough to reveal the restless, insecure boy beneath. “Imported? I’ll have you know my grandmother was from the Rhondda.” “Was she?” Gwenna tilted her head, her gaze drifting unimpressed down his immaculate Italian lapels. “Did she teach you to stand about posturing while dripping rainwater all over an 1890 edition of George Borrow?” He stepped back as if stung, his hands going up defensively. “I’m not posturing. I was merely… making conversation.” He rubbed the back of his neck, the theatricality suddenly draining away, replaced by an earnest, exasperated pout. “Look, do you really not—? Never mind. It doesn't matter.” Gwenna almost smiled. The sudden collapse of his swagger was devastatingly endearing. She fought the urge to soften, her fingers digging into the wool of her sleeves. “Tea?” she asked. Julian blinked. “What?” “I’ve a kettle on the back stove. You look like a drowned spaniel.” “A drowned— I am an artist,” he muttered, though the offended edge in his voice lacked any real bite. He watched her slip off the stool. “Milk, please. No sugar.” She disappeared into the back alcove. Julian stood in the quiet shop, listening to the clatter of mugs, feeling strangely off-kilter. Usually, by minute three, people were asking for selfies or looking flustered. She was entirely immune. It drove him mad. It made him want to stand on the counter and recite Shakespeare until she looked at him with something resembling awe. His eyes fell to the desk. Beside her ledger lay a wooden tackle box, open to reveal brass scales, small camel-hair brushes, a pocket microscope, and several neatly labeled wax-paper packets. Julian leaned closer. He frowned, his curiosity piqued. He reached out and nudged one of the packets with a finger. When Gwenna returned, balancing two mismatched mugs, she found him bent double over the desk, nose practically touching the wood. “Careful,” she said sharply. “Those are delicate.” “*Boletus edulis*?” Julian asked without looking up. He pointed a long, slender finger at a pale, dried cross-section. “No, wait. Pores are too yellow for a young cep. Is that… a birch bolete? Look at the scrobiculations on the stipe.” Gwenna froze, nearly slopping Earl Grey onto the floorboards. She set the mugs down with a soft clack. “*Leccinum scabrum*,” she corrected, her voice losing its guarded dry edge. “Harvested near the reservoir on Tuesday.” Julian looked up, his eyes wide and completely stripped of his earlier artifice. “You’re a forager.” “I am,” she said, caught off guard. “Don't tell me you eat wild fungi. Hollywood actors only consume activated almonds and sunlight, surely.” Julian scoffed, picking up his mug and ignoring the barb. “Hollywood can keep its almonds. There’s nothing on earth like finding a flush of chanterelles hidden under beech leaf litter after a hard frost. My uncle kept a cottage in Sussex. Used to drag me out at dawn with a wicker basket and an Opinel knife.” He leaned in, the actor forgotten, replaced by genuine zeal. “Tell me you have a spot for horn of plenty around here. I’ve been craving *Craterellus cornucopioides* for three months, and the hotel chef in Cardiff looked at me like I’d asked him to cook a shoe.” Gwenna stared at him. The arrogant veneer was utterly gone; his face was open, animated, lit from within by pure, unadulterated nerdiness. Her stomach did that dangerous flip again, much more violently this time. “Black trumpets?” she whispered, leaning forward over the counter despite herself. “Two miles up the valley. Under the old oaks by the stream.” “You’re lying.” Julian was inches from her now, leaning over the display, his gaze locked onto hers. The space between them crackled with an entirely new, electric friction. “They’re nearly impossible to spot in the wet.” “Not if you know how to look for the shadows instead of the caps,” Gwenna murmured. She swallowed, suddenly excruciatingly aware of the gold flecks in his dark eyes, and how close his mouth was to hers. Her breath hitched. Julian saw it—the slight parting of her lips, the subtle flush that climbed the graceful curve of her throat. For once in his life, he didn't feel the smug thrill of victory. He just felt an ache, sudden and heavy, right in the center of his chest. “Show me,” he said, his voice dropping to a rough, genuine whisper. “When the rain stops. Take me with you.” Gwenna held his gaze, her defensive walls crumbling into the quiet scent of damp paper and Earl Grey. “Maybe,” she said softly, picking up her pencil again, though her fingers trembled just enough for him to see. “If you buy a book first.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates the requested Welsh setting, establishes the meet-cute scenario with paparazzi pursuit, and develops both characters according to their specified archetypes. Julian is portrayed as a charming rogue with fragile ego needs, while Gwenna maintains surface immunity to his charms while being inwardly affected. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Julian's theatrical, slightly pompous speech patterns contrast well with Gwenna's dry, understated Welsh sensibility. The author shows skill in revealing character through speech - Julian's desperate need for validation comes through in his increasingly elaborate attempts at charm, while Gwenna's defenses are evident in her clipped responses. The turning point around mycology (mushroom foraging) is genuinely surprising and well-executed. It provides a believable foundation for their connection that transcends superficial attraction. This shared passion allows both characters to drop their guards authentically, creating earned romantic tension. The prose quality is generally high, with evocative descriptions of the Welsh setting and effective use of sensory details. The author demonstrates restraint in avoiding excessive purple prose while maintaining atmospheric richness. The pacing builds naturally from Julian's frantic entrance to the quieter, more intimate moments over tea. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Certain phrases veer toward overwrought territory ("the cold little voice that whispered they're not looking at you grazed his ribs"). Some character insights feel slightly told rather than shown, particularly regarding Gwenna's internal reactions. The transformation from antagonistic banter to romantic tension, while well-motivated by the mycology revelation, happens quite rapidly. The ending strikes an appropriate note - romantic possibility without premature resolution. The chemistry feels earned through their shared intellectual passion rather than mere physical attraction. The piece successfully balances the requested character dynamics while creating genuine emotional engagement. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The heavy, iron-strapped oak door yielded with a wet groan, parting the reek of damp limestone and rendered spermaceti that curdled in the depths of the Morska underhold. Aya stepped through first, her boots silent on the slime-slick flagstones. Behind her, Katra’s breath came in shallow, ragged rasps, while Simeon hovered at her flank, clutching a cold-iron crowbar like a drowning man to timber. From the pocket of Simeon’s embroidered, oil-stained waistcoat, a brass pocket watch ticked. *Clack-tick. Clack-tick.* In the suffocating stillness beneath the city, the escapement sounded like dry bones rattling in a tin cup. "Douse the lamp," Aya whispered through the black linen of her cowl. "The vault should be three paces past the—" A lantern shutter snapped open. Blinding, amber brilliance flooded the chamber, thick with the oily yellow smoke of burning blubber. Aya’s eyes burned, her night-adjusted vision washing out into searing white. "Past the drainage sluice, were you going to say, pet?" The voice was like stones grinding in an iron churn. Aya froze. Her vision resolved, piecing together the nightmare before her. There, seated upon an upturned tallow cask before the Scythan vault, was Madam Vesper. Decidedly un-arrested. Decidedly whole. She wore her voluminous coat of boiled leviathan hide, the lapels stiffened with salt and dried gore, a heavy, brass-bound wheellock pistol resting idly across her knees. Flanking her were six men—dock-rats and cutthroats—their pneumatic harpoon-carbines already raised, iron triggers primed. The copper pressure reservoirs hissed softly, a chorus of coiled serpents. *A trap,* the cold voice in Aya’s mind whispered. *Not a raid. A purge.* "Drop the iron, lad," Vesper drawled, nodding at Simeon. "Before Mr. Gault puts six inches of serrated steel through your spleen. It’s a devil of a mess to scrub out of the mortar." Simeon’s crowbar clattered to the stones. He went stiff, his hands fluttering upward. *Clack-tick. Clack-tick.* His watch continued its relentless, nervous countdown against his ribs. Two hulking brutes stepped from the shadows of the vaulted arches, smelling of cheap gin and bilge water. Steel was thrust hard into Katra’s throat, and she choked back a sob as she was kicked to her knees. Rough, calloused hands seized Aya by the collar, wrenching her arms behind her back with enough force to pop the shoulder joint. A snub-nosed pistol pressed against the hollow beneath her ear—cold, oily, and brutally mechanical. Aya did not summon the immateria. The void-realm stirred beneath the floorboards, cold and bottomless, begging for the slit in reality through which it could pour. But men of the Morska did not hesitate before witches. They did not pause to listen to incantations. They trusted brass, oil, and twelve-gauge lead shot, and at this range, a bullet would tear her skull apart before the shadows could even coalesce into teeth. Her mother had hesitated before the magistrates’ muskets; Aya would not make the same mistake. Madam Vesper rose, her cane—tipped with carved whalebone—clicking sharply on the stone as she limped forward. "I wondered which of my little rats would smell the cheese first," Vesper purred. She reached out, her thick fingers, stained permanent black from machinery grease, taking hold of Aya’s cowl. With a sharp tug, she ripped it away. Aya’s pale face and dark, meticulously pinned hair spilled into the lantern light. Fine bone structure. Skin untouched by the sun, the dockyards, or the rickets. Vesper stared. A slow, revolted smile pulled at the scarred flesh of the guild leader's mouth. "Well, damn my eyes and call me a saint," Vesper chuckled, gesturing with the barrel of her pistol. "Look at the porcelain doll. Look at the little lordling’s daughter playing in the gutter." Aya’s heart battered against her ribs like a bird in a chimney. *No. God, no.* If her identity slipped past these walls—if House Danvers was tied to the Morska Guild—she wouldn’t simply be disowned. The Inquisitors of the Ministry of Steam and Pyre would come for her, just as they had come for her mother. They would search her rooms. They would find the sigils carved into her bedposts, the jars of preserved spirit-flesh, the immateria ink. They would hang her from the high gibbet over the harbor, letting the salt gulls pluck out her eyes. "Tie them," Vesper ordered casually, turning her back. "Slit the throats of the other two and toss 'em in the harbor. As for our blue-blooded phantom here... the rendering vats are running hot tonight. She’ll melt down to grease just like the rest of us." "Wait!" Aya’s voice cut through the hiss of the steam pipes. It was not the muffled, raspy tone she used on the streets; it was the crisp, crystalline cadence of the upper spires. Imperious. Desperate. Vesper paused, looking over her shoulder. "Giving orders, ladybird?" *Clack-tick. Clack-tick.* "You kill me, and you burn a fortune," Aya said, holding her chin high despite the heavy fist still tangled in her hair. "You think you’re safe, Vesper? You bought off the Harbor Watch to fake your arrest, but how much did it cost you? Half the guild’s treasury? Three-quarters?" A flicker of irritation crossed Vesper’s weathered face. A hit. "I am the eldest daughter of Lord Cassian Danvers," Aya pressed, the words tasting like poison on her tongue. The ruin of her life, offered up on a platter. "The High Commissioner of Naval Contracts. You know his name. You know his seal." "I know he hangs thieves," Vesper spat. "He pays ransoms for his own blood," Aya countered, her gaze boring into the guild leader’s dead eyes. "Ten thousand sovereigns. Quietly. Handed over at the lower docks with no Watch intervention. More than this whole miserable guild earns in a season. Kill me, and my father’s personal guard will turn this underhold into a slaughterhouse within the week. Keep me alive, and you buy the whole damn district." Vesper stared at her for three agonizing beats. *Clack-tick. Clack-tick.* The guild leader stepped close, the sulfurous tang of her breath washing over Aya’s face. She raised the heavy brass pistol, resting the warm, smoking barrel against Aya's aristocratic cheekbone. "Ten thousand," Vesper murmured, calculating. Her eyes drifted to Katra and Simeon, then back to Aya. "A pretty sum for a pretty neck. But if your father sniffs a trap, girl... I won’t just hang you. I’ll peel the skin off you for boot leather, and feed what's left to the harbor eels." Vesper lowered the gun and stepped back. "Chain them in the iron cells. All three. And take that bloody watch off the lad before I smash it into his forehead."

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric worldbuilding within the whalepunk fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid, grimy Victorian-industrial environment with evocative details like "reek of damp limestone and rendered spermaceti," "pneumatic harpoon-carbines," and "brass-bound wheellock pistol." The worldbuilding feels authentic and immersive, effectively blending steampunk technology with maritime elements. The adherence to instructions is excellent - all story beats are hit precisely: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-incarcerated guild leader, Aya is captured and unmasked, and she attempts to negotiate using her aristocratic value as leverage. The dialogue authentically captures the gritty Victorian aesthetic, particularly in Vesper's voice ("damn my eyes and call me a saint," "ladybird," "blue-blooded phantom"). Character voices are well-differentiated and consistent. Vesper emerges as a compelling antagonist with her crude, calculating manner, while Aya's desperation and quick thinking come through clearly. The internal conflict about revealing her identity feels genuine and stakes-appropriate. The supporting characters, while less developed, serve their roles effectively. The prose quality is generally high, with strong sensory details and atmospheric description. The recurring motif of Simeon's pocket watch ("Clack-tick. Clack-tick.") effectively builds tension. However, some descriptions venture into purple prose territory - phrases like "cold voice in Aya's mind whispered" and "heart battered against her ribs like a bird in a chimney" feel somewhat overwrought. The dialogue is the piece's strongest element, feeling natural and character-appropriate. Vesper's threats are menacing without being cartoonish, and Aya's desperate negotiation feels authentic to her aristocratic background and current predicament. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension effectively from the quiet entrance through the revelation and confrontation. The emotional complexity is solid - Aya's internal struggle between self-preservation and protecting her companions, her fear of exposure, and her calculated risk-taking all feel earned. Some minor weaknesses include occasional over-description that slows momentum, and a few instances where the gothic atmosphere feels slightly forced rather than organic. The ending, while appropriate, doesn't offer much surprise beyond the expected outcome of the negotiation. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bar smells like spilled tequila, stale mop water, and old blood. Overhead, a ceiling fan lazily slices through a thick haze of cigarette smoke, doing nothing to cut the tropical humidity clinging to the room. Spike Spiegel sits slumped over a scarred wooden counter, his long legs folded under the stool. He swirls a glass of lukewarm bourbon, watching the ice melt into amber water. Two stools down, sitting with her combat boots hooked into the rung and a bottle of rum dangling from two fingers, is a woman who looks like she was forged in a blast furnace. Cutoff denim, a black crop top, and a dragon tattoo slithering up her right arm. Twin modified Beretta 92Fs—customized long-slide Cutlasses—rest snugly in shoulder holsters beneath her open shirt. Revy takes a drag off her smoke, exhales through her nose, and turns her dark amber eyes toward him. "You’ve been staring for ten minutes, afro. You got an itch, or are you just admiring the hardware?" Spike raises his glass in a lazy half-toast, his mismatched eyes half-lidded. "A little of both. Mostly wondering if you know that the guy with the five-million-woolong bounty on his head isn't coming through that door tonight." Revy’s smirk hardens into a predatory sneer. "Ten million baht, pal. And he is coming. Unless some scruffy tourist in a yellow shirt decides to get in my way." "Blue suit," Spike corrects mildly, tapping the ash from his bent cigarette. "And I don't get in the way. I just let things drift." "Yeah? Well, drift your ass outside before I blow a vent through that fluffy mop of yours." Before Spike can offer another dry quip, the swinging doors splinter off their hinges. Four men in cheap linen suits enter with submachine guns, scanning the dimly lit dive. The leader points a heavy barrel straight at Revy. "Neither of you is getting the money," the lead goon barks. Revy doesn’t blink. She doesn't hesitate. Her Cutlasses clear leather in a silver blur, barking twin streaks of fire before the goon even finishes drawing a breath. His chest explodes in crimson. Spike moves like water. He slips off the stool in a fluid roll as lead tears the bar to splinters. Kicking the heavy oak stool, he launches it into the face of a second gunman with a sickening crunch. He draws his Jericho 941 in the same motion, placing two neat rounds through the man’s center mass before he hits the floor. Revy is already laughing—a manic, throat-scraping sound. She pivots, ducking under a spray of plaster, and pumps three rounds into the third man, walking him backward against the wall. The fourth man scrambles for the exit, but Spike intercepts him, sweeping the man's legs out from under him with a graceful sweep and planting the heel of his boot into the man's throat. Silence settles, punctured only by the hiss of a ruptured beer tap and the frantic spinning of spent brass on the tile. Revy lowers her smoking guns, her chest heaving against her top. She looks at Spike, whose hair hasn't even fallen out of place, a half-burned smoke still clinging miraculously to his lower lip. Her lips curl. "Not bad, pretty boy. You move fast for a corpse." "You're loud," Spike replies, tucking the Jericho back into his jacket. "And you waste ammo." Revy scoffs, spitting blood-tinged saliva onto the sawdust. "Efficiency is for tight-asses. Come on. The cops in this shithole take twenty minutes to finish their donuts, but I’d rather not deal with the paperwork." *** The neon sign outside the motel buzzes a sickly pink, casting harsh shadows across the peeling wallpaper of room 204. The rain has started, a relentless tropical deluge rattling against the cracked windowpane. Spike sits on the edge of the mattress, digging a Zippo from his pocket. A distinct ring of rust around the lighter’s brass casing suggests it has been dropped in water more than once—perhaps salt spray, perhaps a river in another life. He flicks it. The flame catches on the second try, illuminating the sharp angles of his face as he lights a fresh cigarette. Revy stands by the rickety dresser, draining the last dregs from a pocket flask. She watches him through heavy eyelids. The adrenaline hasn't faded; it’s curdled into something hotter, thick with the scent of rain, cheap whiskey, and spent gunpowder. "The bounty's datapad is in your pocket," Revy says, her voice low, raspy. She leans against the wall, crossing her arms beneath her chest. "Drop it on the dresser, and maybe I don't put a hole in you while you sleep." "I don't sleep much," Spike says smoothly, blowing a thin plume of smoke toward the ceiling. "And splitting it fifty-fifty sounds a lot less messy." "I don't share," she snaps, stepping closer. The air between them tightens, electric and suffocating. She stops just inches from where he sits, looking down at him. There's a raw, jagged hunger in her eyes—the look of a stray that bites any hand offering food, yet aches for the touch anyway. "And I sure as hell don't trust a guy who looks at me like he’s already halfway in the grave." Spike looks up at her. His right eye reflects the pink neon outside; his left eye seems lost in a different, colder world. He reaches out with agonizing slowness, his fingers brushing against the rough denim at her hip, tracing the cold steel of the Cutlass still holstered there. Revy’s breath catches, but she doesn't pull away. "You talk a lot of violence for someone who followed me up the stairs," he murmurs. "Maybe I just wanted to see what you were made of," she whispers fiercely, leaning down until her lips are an inch from his, her warm, bourbon-laced breath brushing his cheek. "Turns out it's mostly smoke." "Could be," Spike says. In the span of a single heartbeat, the atmosphere snaps. Revy’s hand drops to her holster, drawing with terrifying speed, but Spike is already moving. He twists, his palm slamming upward to deflect her wrist, while his left hand clears his jacket. A hard, metallic click echoes through the tiny room. Revy’s Beretta is pressed dead center against Spike’s forehead, the cold muzzle leaving a red indentation in his skin. Spike’s Jericho is wedged firmly beneath Revy’s chin, forcing her head slightly back. Neither flinches. Their bodies are pressed flush against each other, chests rising and falling in sync, tangled in a deadly, intimate gridlock. Revy’s dark eyes burn with a feral spark, a wild, crooked grin spreading across her lips. Spike’s mouth curves into a faint, reckless smirk. "You're crazy," Spike says, his thumb resting gently on the hammer of his gun. "Takes one to know one, cowboy," she breathes, her finger curling tight against her trigger. Her pulse hammers against the steel of his barrel. Outside, thunder cracks, rattling the glass. Inside, neither pulls the trigger, and neither lowers their weapon. They just breathe each other in, waiting for the first mistake. "Whatever happens, happens," Spike whispers. Revy chuckles darkly. "You bet your dead ass it does."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and faithful character portrayal within the crossover premise. The author successfully captures both Spike's laconic fatalism and Revy's volatile aggression, maintaining their distinct voices throughout. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, with Spike's dry observations ("You're loud. And you waste ammo") contrasting effectively with Revy's crude directness. The action sequence in the bar is well-choreographed, showcasing each character's combat style appropriately - Revy's dual-wielding aggression versus Spike's fluid martial arts approach. The pacing builds effectively from the initial tension to the climactic standoff. The atmospheric details work well, from the seedy bar's "spilled tequila, stale mop water, and old blood" to the motel's "sickly pink" neon. The author demonstrates restraint in not over-describing while still establishing mood effectively. However, the piece suffers from some predictability in its structure - the bar shootout and motel standoff follow fairly expected beats for this type of story. The sexual tension, while present, relies heavily on familiar tropes of the "enemies who might be lovers" dynamic without adding much fresh insight. The ending standoff is dramatically effective but somewhat expected given the setup. The mutual gun-pointing scene has been done many times before, though it's executed competently here. The piece delivers exactly what was promised but doesn't transcend its genre conventions. The prose occasionally veers toward overwrought territory with phrases like "forged in a blast furnace" and some of the more elaborate action descriptions, but generally maintains good control. The character work is the strongest element, with both protagonists feeling true to their source material while functioning believably in this new context. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Even now, thirty years later, I cannot sit in total darkness without keeping my back pressed firmly against a wall. In October of 1995, I was fifteen and miserable, dragged from the electric hum of Stockholm to an iron-grey parish in Västerbotten where my father had been appointed mill administrator. The village was little more than a sprawl of clapboard houses swallowed by spruce. My world had shrunk to the four walls of my attic bedroom, the static hiss of my Walkman, and Astrid. Astrid was the only girl in school who didn’t smell of damp wool and cow barns. She smelled like clove cigarettes and stale sea-water. She claimed her maternal grandmother had been an *åkallare*—a caller—and had left behind notebooks written in a jagged, crabbed hand. To me, bored half to death, Astrid’s games were merely an extension of the Ouija boards we used at sleepovers back south: a thrilling, half-believed pretense designed to extract teenage secrets. We had already chanted over bowls of stagnant ditch water to find out who had slashed the gym teacher’s tires, and burned braids of dried yarrow behind the hockey rink to make Pelle Lindqvist notice her. It was all theatre. Until the mound. "It’s called *útiseta*," she told me behind the bus shed that Tuesday, biting the skin around her thumbnail until it bled. Her eyes, pale as dirty ice, held mine. "It means 'sitting out.' The old ones sat out on mounds to make the *draug* talk. To ask for song, or prophecy, or to see whose thread is snapping next." "It’s an old grave, Astrid. It’s dirt." "It’s a door," she whispered, leaning in so I could smell the menthol on her tongue. "Sofia Holmström thinks she’s untouchable because her dad runs the bank. Don’t you want to know what she did at the midsummer cabin? The mound knows the blood spilled in this valley. We sit until the third hour. We ask, and it answers." She made it sound like borrowing an illicit cassette tape. We snuck out at eleven. The autumn frost had silvered the gravel roads, crunching loudly beneath our Doc Martens. We walked past the village limits, where the sodium lamps gave out and the boreal forest closed around the road like a black fist. The mound lay half a kilometer into the brush, an unmistakable, artificial swell in the peat—an Iron Age tumulus overgrown with bilberry scrub and spindly, choking birch. Local folklore held that a chieftain lay buried beneath the sod, though the state archaeologists had never bothered to dig. Astrid took charge with an eerie, clinical efficiency that unsettled me far more than her teenage posturing ever had. She pulled an iron hunting knife from the pocket of her oversized flannel and drove it cleanly through the frozen turf at the crest of the mound. "Iron binds," she muttered, her breath misting between us. She smoothed out an unbleached linen sheet across the frozen ground. "Sit cross-legged. Knees touching mine. Once your seat is taken, you do not shift your hips. You do not speak until you hear your own tongue spoken back to you. And if you feel fingers working at the laces of your boots, Linnea, you ignore them." "Astrid, this is stupid," I said, a shiver chasing the bravado from my voice. The cold was already biting through my corduroys. "Sit," she hissed. Her face was entirely blank, stripped of the smirking irreverence she wore at school. I sat. The turf beneath the linen was spongy, unnervingly soft compared to the frosted rock around us. It felt almost warm, like a compost pile fermenting in the deep earth. Astrid sat opposite me, her knees wedged against mine, our hands resting flat on our thighs. We waited. Minutes dissolved into the heavy, resinous dark. I tried to focus on normal things—the math test on Friday, the lyrics to the Cranberries song stuck in my head—but the forest seemed to warp scale and time. The dark was not empty; it had weight. It pressed against the drums of my ears like deep water. The wind occasionally rustled the pine trees, sounding almost like faint whispers. At first, I told myself it was just that: the boreal draft sweeping down from Lapland, filtered through millions of stiff pine needles. But as the stillness dragged on, the cadence felt deliberate. Sibilant syllables rose and dipped just beyond my range of hearing, teasing the margins of sense. *S-k-a... v-e-t...* My legs went numb. An itch blossomed on my collarbone, agonizing in its intensity, but Astrid’s gaze pinned me. Her eyes were wide, unblinking, reflecting the pale smudge of the moon. Her chest barely rose. Then came the vibration. It was faint—a low-frequency thrum that did not enter through my ears, but rose straight through my tailbone from the bowels of the earth. A rhythmic, subterranean heave, like a gigantic lung expanding beneath centuries of compacted peat. *Pelle had a tractor,* I thought frantically, desperately seeking logic. *Someone is running an engine on the south logging trail.* Yet the cadence was too slow, too organic. It rose and fell like a sleeper turning over. The whispers in the pines shifted. They were no longer in the canopy; they seemed to circle the base of the mound, moving through the heather at the speed of a walking man. The smell changed, too—the clean, pine-needle air curdled into a thick stench of stagnant ditch water, wet wool, and old rot. Astrid’s right eyelid began to twitch. A bead of sweat, brilliant silver in the gloom, traced the line of her jaw. *Break the circle,* my mind screamed. *Stand up and run.* But the paralysis was absolute. It was the crushing weight of sleep apnea, or hypothermia setting into my starved muscles. I stared at the linen between us. In the dim light, the white cloth appeared to be depressing slightly between our knees, two rounded indentations sinking into the fabric, as if a third person were kneeling there, facing the iron knife. A voice sighed. It did not come from the wind, nor Astrid, nor the woods. It rose from the dirt directly beneath my palms, vibrating against my flesh. It was thin, dry as dried lichen, and utterly without moisture. It spoke a name. Not Sofia’s. Not Pelle’s. It spoke my grandmother’s maiden name—a name I had never once uttered aloud in Västerbotten, a name buried three hundred miles away in an urn in Uppland. Astrid gasped, the sound like tearing paper. Her hand shot out, knocking the iron knife sideways in the dirt. The silence that followed was violent. The thrum ceased. The whispering pines went dead and still. We scrambled down the mound on our hands and knees, tearing our jeans on the briars, running toward the glow of the road with our lungs burning like battery acid. We didn’t look back. We didn’t speak of it the next morning, or the week after, or ever. In the light of day, I told myself it was carbon monoxide from the bog, or mass hysteria, or a cruel acoustic trick of the northern wind. I told myself Astrid had peeked at my mother’s mail when she visited my house. I told myself all of that. But I never touched Astrid’s hands again, and even now, I will not walk on ground that swells without a reason.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric control in the folk horror genre. The author successfully establishes the required setting of rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s, with authentic details like the mill administrator father, Västerbotten location, and cultural references (Doc Martens, Walkman, Cranberries). The first-person retrospective narration is handled skillfully, with the adult perspective subtly informing the teenage experience without overwhelming it. The characterization is nuanced and believable. Linnea's evolution from bored Stockholm teenager to genuinely frightened participant feels authentic, and her rationalizations ring true. Astrid is particularly well-crafted - the shift from teenage posturing to eerie clinical efficiency during the ritual creates genuine unease. The author avoids making her a simple "spooky girl" archetype by grounding her in realistic details like clove cigarettes and menthol breath. The prose quality is consistently high, with evocative imagery that serves the horror atmosphere without becoming overwrought. Phrases like "iron-grey parish," "the dark had weight," and "crushing weight of sleep apnea" create visceral sensations. The author demonstrates restraint in building tension, allowing the supernatural elements to emerge gradually rather than rushing toward shock moments. The ritual itself is convincingly researched and presented. The útiseta concept feels authentic, and the specific details (iron knife, linen sheet, positioning) create believability. The ambiguity between psychological and supernatural explanations is maintained effectively - the carbon monoxide theory and other rational explanations remain plausible while the supernatural elements feel genuinely unsettling. The pacing builds tension methodically, from the initial setup through the mounting dread of the ritual to the climactic moment when the voice speaks the grandmother's maiden name. This detail is particularly effective because it's specific enough to feel genuinely impossible to explain away, yet subtle enough to avoid melodrama. The ending strikes an appropriate tone for folk horror - the characters flee, never speak of it again, but remain permanently changed. The adult narrator's admission about avoiding swelling ground and keeping her back to walls provides satisfying psychological aftermath without over-explaining. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable elements in the setup (the bored city girl befriending the mysterious local) and occasional moments where the prose approaches purple territory, though it generally pulls back before crossing that line. The piece also adheres closely to folk horror conventions without significantly subverting them, though this may be appropriate given the prompt's requirements. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The vinyl of the treatment table was cold through the thin paper runner, sticking to the backs of my thighs. Everything in the clinic was white and brushed aluminum—a deliberate, antiseptic contrast to the chalk-dusted rubber and sweat-soaked iron where Julian and I had spent our twenties. Julian stood at the foot of the plinth, uncapping a tub of mobilization cream. On his forearms, he still wore them: the compression sleeves, a riot of violently bright teal and violet polygons. They were the same custom sleeves from our 2021 Olympic Trials camp. On him, they were a nostalgic quirk, the eccentric styling of a decorated 400-meter hurdler who had gracefully transitioned into a doctorate of physical therapy. On me, my old kit was buried in the back of a closet, a shroud for a career that ended when my right knee buckled over the fifth hurdle in Zurich. "Supine, Maya," he said. His voice was level, dialed into that infuriatingly measured clinical cadence. "Let’s see where the graft is holding before we stress the capsule." I lay flat on my back. My right leg felt like an alien apparatus attached to my hip—stiff, swollen, and carved with three pale, raised surgical portals and a six-inch vertical scar over the patellar tendon. Julian stepped forward. His hip brushed the edge of the low table, close enough that I caught the clean, cedar scent of his collar beneath the clinic’s isopropyl wash. When his bare fingers made contact with my distal thigh, just above the superior border of the patella, my quadriceps twitched in an involuntary, defensive spasm. "Breathe out," he murmured. "Don't fight the baseline." His left hand stabilized my distal femur while the heel of his right palm found the inferior pole of my kneecap. He applied a firm, downward inferior glide to clear the scar tissue anchoring the joint. A hot, sickening needle of pain spiked under the bone, radiating down the tibia. My hands gripped the edges of the table, knuckles whitening. "Still adhered," he noted, clinical, completely detached from the agony he was methodically manufacturing. Yet his thumbs were warm, his fingers broad and calloused. As he worked the patella medially, then laterally, his forearms flexed, the vivid geometric fabric shifting over tight radial muscle. I watched the tendon cord in his neck. There had been a night in Eugene four years ago, after the 4x400 relay, where that same cord had pressed against my collarbone in a poorly lit hotel room. We had never spoken of it. We had gone back to our respective lanes. Now, he was whole, thriving, and my leg was a ruined piece of meat he was manipulating for sixty-five dollars an hour. "I can do the mobilizations myself with the strap," I said, my voice clipped, breathless from the pressure. "You can't achieve this angle of glide with a strap, and you know it," he said without looking up. He released my knee. The sudden absence of pain was a vacuum, replaced instantly by the hyper-awareness of where his hands lingered on the bare skin above my joint. "Leg up. Hamstring progression," he directed. He positioned himself on the right side of the plinth, facing me. He slid his right arm beneath my lower leg, scooping under the Achilles, and lifted my right heel from the table. My knee remained locked in full extension. With his left hand resting flat over the anterior surface of my distal thigh to prevent compensatory flexion, he raised my leg vertically. Thirty degrees. Forty-five. At sixty degrees, the scarred tissue behind the popliteal fossa screamed. The hamstring origin at my ischial tuberosity pulled taut like a steel cable. "Tell me when," he said softly. "Keep going." "Maya." "I said keep going." He took a step forward, closing the distance between us until his left hip was flush against the edge of the table, between my splayed left leg and the elevated right. He brought my heel up, resting the back of my ankle directly against the hollow of his left shoulder. The proximity was suffocating. I could see the tiny amber flecks in his irises, the slight stubble along his jawline, the rhythmic pulse in the notch of his throat. His hand slid down from my quad to pin my pelvis, fingers spreading wide over my anterior superior iliac spine to keep my hips square. The heat of his palm seared through my running shorts. "Isometric contraction," he instructed, his breath grazing my shin. "Drive your heel back down into my shoulder. Twenty percent effort. Hold for six." I fired the hamstring. My heel dug into the solid meat of his trapezius. I felt the dense resistance of his body absorbing my force—unyielding, stable, infuriatingly strong. My eyes locked onto his. There was no clinical detachment in the strain of his neck, in the way his pupils dilated as our physical effort mirrored the brutal sprint drills of our past. "Two. One. Relax," he exhaled. I released the contraction. Instantly, Julian leaned his torso forward, using the weight of his own chest to push my ankle past eighty degrees, dragging my leg deeper into flexion. The pain was exquisite, a white-hot line of tension that made my back arch off the table. A ragged gasp broke from my mouth. My left hand shot out, involuntarily grabbing his upper arm, my fingers digging into the bright compression sleeve, feeling the rock-hard swell of his tricep beneath. Julian didn't flinch, nor did he pull back. He held me suspended at the razor's edge of tissue tolerance, his chest pressing my foot toward my head, his hand anchored heavy and hot against my hip. For four endless seconds, we stayed pinned in that violent, intimate geometry. His eyes dropped to my lips, parted and drawing shallow air, before flicking back to mine. The tension in the room wasn't just the tensile limit of a repaired tendon; it was the suffocating weight of everything we had both lost and refused to mourn. "Good," he whispered, his voice suddenly thicker, losing its antiseptic veneer. "That's ninety-two degrees." He backed off millimeter by millimeter, letting my heel slide down from his shoulder into his cradling hands. He lowered the limb to the vinyl with meticulous, agonized slowness, never breaking physical contact until my heel met the table. He stepped back, clearing his throat and adjusting the waistband of his trousers. The geometric sleeves seemed absurdly bright under the fluorescent tubes. "Roll onto your stomach," he said, turning toward the ultrasound cart, his back to me, his shoulders rising and falling on a slow, controlled intake of air. "We need to work the scar."

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical proficiency in meeting the prompt's demanding requirements. The author successfully navigates the complex challenge of maintaining anatomical precision while building sexual tension through therapeutic contact. The first-person narrative voice is consistently maintained throughout, capturing Maya's bitter resentment toward her circumstances while revealing her conflicted attraction to Julian. The characterization is nuanced, avoiding simple archetypes. Maya's anger at her situation feels authentic, as does Julian's professional struggle to maintain boundaries with someone from his past. The backstory is efficiently woven in through specific details like the compression sleeves and the Eugene hotel room reference. The prose quality is notably high, with sophisticated sentence structure and precise word choice. Medical terminology is seamlessly integrated without feeling forced or show-offy. The sensory details are vivid and specific—the vinyl table, isopropyl wash scent, and the geometric patterns on Julian's sleeves all contribute to immersive world-building. The sexual tension builds organically through the physical therapy context rather than feeling artificially imposed. The author skillfully uses the legitimate therapeutic need for intimate contact to create charged moments, particularly during the hamstring stretch sequence where Julian's positioning creates unavoidable proximity. However, the piece occasionally veers toward purple prose, particularly in phrases like "exquisite pain" and "violent, intimate geometry." Some descriptions, while technically proficient, feel slightly overwrought. The ending, while maintaining the established tension, doesn't offer much surprise in its trajectory. The dialogue, though limited, feels natural and serves the clinical setting well. Julian's professional language contrasting with moments of personal breakthrough works effectively. The piece maintains coherence throughout and doesn't meander despite its detailed focus on physical procedures.
